full_judgment:
2. Facts necessary for the disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the opposite parties Nos. Ito 4, 6, predecessor of opposite parties No.5 (a) to 5(h) and predecessor of opposite parties No. 7(a) to (e) as plaintiffs instituted Small Causes Court (SCC) Suit No. 2 of 1988 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court and S.C.C. Judge, Sylhet, against one Abdul Wahid, predecessor of the present defendant /petitioners, who was a monthly tenant under the predecessor of the plaintiffs/ opposite parties, for eviction from the suit premises for defaulting in paying rent and on the ground of bonafide requirement of the suit premises. During the pendency-of the suit Abdul Wahid, the sole defendant died on 03. 10.1995 and the present petitioners were substituted as his legal heirs. Thereafter, the original plaintiff Nos. 5 and 7 also died during the pendency of the suit and their legal heirs, plaintiff No. 5(a) to 5 (h) and 7(a) to 7 (e) were also substituted as plaintiffs in their places. It is alleged in the plaint of the SCC Suit that the deceased Abdul Wahid took monthly lease of the suit premises from the predecessor of the plaintiffs, late Jobeda Khatun, by executing a 'Bharanama agreement' dated 03. 10. 1979 at a rental of TK. 450/- per month payable within 5th day of the next following month according to the English. Calendar. The said landlady during the subsistence of the said tenancy agreement died on 27.8.1987 and as such the tenancy right of the defendant Abdul Wahid stood terminated. But the defendant without vacating the same has been running his business in the tenanted premises as an illegal occupant. Thereafter, on the death of the landlady Jobeda Khatun, her heirs became the owners of the suit premises by inheritance and asserted that with the death of the landlady the tenancy right stood terminated and the tenant became an illegal occupant in the said premises. It is further  alleged that the defendant defaulted in paying rent of the suit premises till his death and as such liable to be evicted from the said premises on the ground of being illegal occupant and default and also for bonafidc requirement of the suit premises for necessary repairing, development and use as office/reception hall and dining room of the plaintiffs' hotel business which had been running under the ownership of the plaintiffs on the adjacent part of the suit premises. It is alleged in the instant revisional application that the plaintiffs accordingly sent a notice on 7.7.1 988 under registered post terminating the tenancy under the provision of Transfer of Property Act 1882 asking the defendant to vacate the suit premises on the expiry of the last day of July. 1988. The notice was received by the defendant Abdul Wahid on 9.7.1988 but he did not vacate the suit premises. Hence, this suit for eviction of the defendant from the suit premises. 

 3. Abdul Wahid, the original defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter alia, that he never defaulted in paying rents and the plea of bonafide requirement of the plaintiffs is untrue and unfounded. After the death of the defendant Abdul Wahid on 3.10.1995 the present petitioners were substituted as defendants as they are the legal heirs and successor of the said Abdul Wahid. The defendant/petitioners filed another written statement on 31.12.1996 denying the material allegations of the plaint contending inter alia that the original defendant Abdul Wahid had been running a business or grocery in the suit premises as a monthly tenant under Jobeda Khatun, the predecessor of the present plaintiffs, since long before, at a rental of TK. 450/- per month payable within 15th day of every month next following, according to the English Calenader. It is further asserted that Jobeda Khatun received TK. 30,000/- on 306 December, 1984 from late Abdul Wahid, the original tenant, as advance rent on condition that it would be adjusted towards the monthly rents but the same had not been adjusted as per promise. The defendants regularly paid rent upto July 1987 and were granted receipts for such payment of rents. The rent for the month of August, 1987 was offered to the plaintiff No. 2 Khondaker Karim Uddin Ahmed, who used to collect rents on behalf of Jobeda Khatun during her life time. But said plaintiff No. 2 having refused to accept the same, Abdul Wahid sent the said rent, on 6.9.1987, by postal money order which the plaintiffs refused to accept on 9.9.1987. After return of the said refused money order the original defendant Abdul Wahid deposited the rent for the said month with the House Rent controller Sylhet in House Rent Case No. 68 of 1987 on 27.9.1987 and thenceforth had been depositing rents with the House Rent Controller, Sylhet in the said case regularly. It is further denied that the plaintiffs had any bonafide requirement of the suit premises and the plea of use of the some as reception room for the boarders of the hotel and dining hall of the said hotel is bogus, unfounded and malafide pleas for causing illegal ejectment of the defendant petitioners. As such it is claimed that the suit for ejectment of the defendants was filed with malafide intention to let out the same to others at an enhanced rate and therefore the SCC suit was liable to be dismissed. 

 7. Mr. J.N. Deb, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the defendants/petitioners upon placing the impugned judgment submits that the plaintiffs having claimed that the relationship between the land lady and the tenant being terminated on the death of the land lady Jobeda Khatun on 27.8.1987, the defendant Abdul Wahid became illegal occupant in the suit premises as such a notice dated 6.7.88, registered on 7.7.88, was served upon the defendant directing him to hand over the possession of the rented property to the plaintiffs by 31.7.88 and also asking the defendant to pay Tk. 25/- per pay from 28.8.87 till 31.7.88 for such illegal occupation of the suit premises and therefore, the clear case made out by the plaintiffs is that the defendants are not the tenants under the plaintiffs. Such an assertion in the plaint clearly made the SCC Suit No. 2 of 1988 as not maintainable. The learned Advocate contends that as the plaintiffs do not admit that the defendants are their tenants, the relief as prayed for in the plaints does not fall within the provision section 15 and Article 4 of the S.C.C. Act, and as such the suit is not maintainable. In this respect Mr. Deb relied on the decision of the case of Managing Director, Rupali Bank Limited and others vs. Tajazal Hossein and others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260 and submits that the Appellate division has held in that case "that the jurisdiction is the root of everything 'and if there is no jurisdiction of the Court to try the suit everything shall fall apart." As such Mr. Dev submits that the suit being not maintainable as SCC suit the SC Court has no jurisdiction to try the instant suit and the. Judgment and order passed by the SCC Judge is a nullity and is liable to be struck down by this court. 

 8. The learned Advocate Mr. J.N. Dev further strenuously argued that learned SCC Judge committed serious illegality in coming to the finding that the irregularity in depositing rent after the institution of the Rent deposit case has implication on the question of alleged default made prior to institution of rent deposit case since the deposit of rent is only referable to the cause of action of the eviction suit. 

 9. The learned Advocate Mr. Deb finally argued that the question of bonafide requirement of the tenanted premises by the plaintiffs for the purpose of using the same as reception room and dining hall and of their hotel is not honest and genuine reason for eviction which the defendants were able to prove by adducing corroborative evidence which the learned SCC Judge did not consider. In this respect the learned Advocate referred of the case of Mst. Shamshennessa Sakeba Bayou and others vs. A.H. Mohsenuddin Ahmed and others, reported 27 DLR 643 and submits that the word bonafide has been defined in the said case as equivalent to honest and a kind of genuine and present need and not a colourable pretext. According to the learned Advocate Mr. Dev, the evidence of the Advocate commissioner as P.W. 3 does not come into any assistance to the plaintiffs as to proof of bonafide requirement and as such the same has not established the claim of the plaintiffs. Mr. Dev contends that since the plaintiffs does into recognize the defendant as tenant, there remains no question of paying rent and default. And as such the impugned judgment and order passed by the SCC Judge 'is not sustainable in law. The learned Advocate prays for making the rule absolute. 

 10. On the other hand the learned Advocate Mr. S.H. Md. Nurul Huda Jaigirder, appearing on behalf to the plaintiff/opposite parties strenuously argued that the notice under section 106 of the transfer of property Act 1882 as well as the plaint itself manifest that the plaintiffs although depicted the defendant as illegal occupant but the law recognizes the defendant as tenant by holding over and as such the total assertion of the Notice and the statement in the plaint would clearly show that the original defendant was tenant under the plaintiff /opposite parties after the death of the original land lady. Because, when the defendants admitted that the defendants are the tenants of the present plaintiffs the question of jurisdiction of the SC Court does not arise because of acquiescence. He submits that the defendants in both their written statements as well as in their evidence categorically admitted that the plaintiffs become their landlords after the demise of the original landlady. The learned Advocate Mr. Jaigirdar further argued that the said plea of maintainability of the SCC suit was never taken by the defendants at an earliest opportunity before the SCC Judge and as such the defendants cannot come up now in the revisional application with a fresh plea that there is no landlord and tenant relationship exist and accordingly the suit under SCC Act is not maintainable. Referring to the case of Ahmed Hossain Chowdhury vs. Zakia Khatun reported in 20 DLR 578, Mr. Jaigirder further contends that the defendants having not repudiated the relationship of landlord and tenant in a lawful manner it cannot be said that the relationship has been terminated. The original landlady although died on 27.8.87 but the notice was served on 7.7.88 asking the defendant to vacate the suit premises by 31.7.88, showing the defendant as an illegal occupants in the premises when nearly eleven months after the death of the landlady the tenancy subsisted and the tenant had been paying rents in the House Rent Controller. The learned Advocate Mr. Jaigirdar next submits that the irregularity in depositing rent with the House Rent Controller after the institution of the rent deposit case is obviously a ground to treat the tenant as defaulter because section 19(1)(b) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991 categorically provided that the tenant shall continue to deposit rent with the House Rent Controller within fortnight till the decree is passed. In this respect he relied on the case of Ramjan Ali Misery Vs. Md. Hedayetullah reported in 31 DLR (AD) 183. 

 11. Mr. Jaigirder further submits that the defendant in their written statement did not plead as to when the refused money order was received by the defendant nor in their evidence they said anything as to such receipt. But apparently on the face of the refused money order (Exhibit -Kha") it appears that the refusal wan made on 9.9.1987 and in the absence of any date mentioned in the written statement, the filing of the House Rent Control (Rent deposit) Case No. 68 of 1987 on depositing the rent on 27.9.1987 is clearly falls beyond the statutory period of 15 days as contemplated in section 19 (1) of the premises Rent Control Act 1991 as such the defendant cannot get any protection of law under the said Act. 

 15. In appreciating the first ground it appears that the plaintiffs did not assert in the plaint that the defendants were tenant under them rather the plaintiffs stated that the original defendant Abdul Wahid was a tenant under Jobeda Khatun, the predecessor of the plaintiffs. It has been alleged in the plaint that with the demise of the plaintiffs' predecessor Jobeda Khatun the bharanama agreement' seized to exist. It further appears from notice dated 7.7.1988 issued for terminating the tenancy that it also does not contain the assertion that the original defendant Abdul Wahid was admitted as a tenant under the plaintiffs rather he was depicted as illegal occupant. But it transpires that the admitted fact is that the original defendant entered into the suit premises on the basis of a `bharanama agreement' entered into with the original landlady and thereafter the landlady died and the plaintiffs entered into the shoes of the landlady as her heirs. It has been alleged that the tenant offered rent for the month of August 1987 to the plaintiff No. 2 who refused to accept the same on 5.9.1978 and thereafter, sent the same by money order on 6.9.78 the same being refused on 9.9.78 the original defendant started depositing the rent with the House Rent Controller Sylhet, in House Rent Case No. 68 of 1987 and continued to pay the same till the House Rent Control case was disposed off. It is also an admitted fact that in the meantime, on 7.7.1988, the plaintiffs issued a notice for eviction upon the defendant which clearly proves that the defendant was admittedly in possession of the suit premises from the date of beginning of the tenancy under the landlady at least till issuance of the notice wherein the defendant was asked to vacate the suit premises by the ends of July 1988. Reading the notice itself and the plaint as a whole, it appears that the defendant was admittedly a tenant under the original landlady and was in possession of the suit premises as such. So the entry of the original defendant in the suit premises was legal who continued to be the lawful tenant till the death of the landlady. Thereafter although, the plaintiffs refused to accept the original defendant as a tenant under them but the provision of section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides that in such a case the tenancy cannot be treated as terminated on the demise of the landlady. It appears that the plaintiffs having inherited the property asked the defendant to vacate the premises after one year of the death of original landlady practically allowing the defendant to deposit the rent with the Rent Controller. Therefore, I hold that admittedly the tenant was neither a trespasser in the suit property nor the relationship of landlord and tenant was terminated. A tenancy for which no term is fixed is a lease running from month to month, terminable upon proper notice. But section 111 of Transfer of Property Act 1882 provides as to the point of time when the relationship terminates. The conditions laid down therein can be a ground for termination of tenancy under such situation. Again there is no provision of law in determining the tenancy on the ground of a tenant becoming an "undesirable tenant" unless a tenant ,comes within the mischief of forfeiture under section H 1(0 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 as decided by their lordships in the Appellate Division in the case of Maria Keshi D' Rozaio vs. Hassan Movies Ltd. reported in 41 DLR (AD) 135. Again section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 can be looked into wherein the nature of such tenant has been described as holding over tenant but question remains that the tenant by holding over in the premises pre suppose a condition that requires acceptance of the rent from the tenant, But in the present case I hold that the tenancy in question is a tenancy by sufferance. Because as the inherited landlords refused to accept the rent from the existing tenant the tenancy cannot be termed as a tenancy by holding over. No doubt the tenant being in possession of the suit premises upon entering into the same as a lawful monthly tenant and had been paying the rent regularly to the original landlady then refusal by the plaintiff No.2 to receive the rent from such tenant made the tenancy a tenancy by sufferance. 

 16. Therefore, I hold that when a tenant remains in possession of the suit premises on termination of a tenancy, due to land lords non-action or negligence in not evicting him to enforce the land lord's right to re-enter, such tenant, who therefore continues his possession by land lord's negative permission is a "tenant by sufferance" who, is not a trespasser nor he could be treated as remaining upon the suit property by wrongful means. In the present case the original land lady died on 27.8.1987 and the defendant was served with notice for eviction on 7.7.1988. So due to negligence of the plaintiffs the tenant was not evicted from the suit premises, who continued paying rents to the House Rent Controller for last eleven months. Moreover, the plaintiffs asked for the premises on bonafide requirement. Thus under all circumstances the tenancy subsists and filing of the suit under the Small Causes Court's Act is very much maintainable and the decision of the Judge of the Small Cause Court is not without lawful authority. That since the suit filed in Small Cause Court is maintainable 1 am of the view that the finding and decision of the trial court i.e. Small Cause Court, arrived at on the basis of the evidences on record are squarely lawful. The argument as advanced by Mr. Deb in this respect fails. 

 17. The contention that the tenancy right is a personal right which ceases with the death of either party may be an age old proposition but the same has been negated by the Appellate Division in the case of Pradip Das Vs. Kazal Das reported in 44 DLR (AD) 1. It transpires that a tenant under the premises Rent Control Ordinance means any person by whom, or on whose account the rent is payable for any premises and includes a legal representative as defined in the Civil Procedure Code. Thus a person continuing in possession after termination of a tenancy, if any, is also a tenant under this definition. Therefore so long the tenancy subsists the same is terminable by notice under section 106 of the Transfer o Property Act 1882 by 15 days notice expiry with the end of a month of the Tenancy Thus the plaintiffs rightly issued notice terminating the tenancy asking the defendant to vacate the suit premises by the end of July 1988. This action of the plaintiffs clearly indicates that the relationship between the landlord and tenant subsisted till 31.7.1988 Moreover, the defendants never denied that Abdul Wahid was not a tenant under the legal representatives of deceased landlady Jobeda Khatun. 

 18. Now turning to the second ground of the plaintiff/ opposite parties let me examine whether the finding of the trial court on the point of default is correct. The trial court in the impugned Judgment observed that admittedly the original defendant paid rent upto July 1987 and the rent for the month of August 1987 was offered to the plaintiff No.2 on 5.9.1987 on the death of the original land lady which was refused by plaintiff No. 2. Thereupon, the 55 day being the Government holiday, on 6.9.1987 the said defendant sent the rent for the month of August 1987 through Money Order to the owner of the house. On perusal of exhibit "Kha" i.e. the Money Order Coupon No. 803 the Court below found that the above statement is correct and it is further found from the said exhibit that the same was refused by the owner on 9.9.1987. But the learned trial Judge found that it is not possible to ascertain as to when the same returned to the said defendant nor it can be -ascertained that the sane returned to defendant on 13.9.1987 because the said exhibit does not contain any date as to when the same was returned to defendant. On a negative approach the Court observed that the D.W.1 did not deny that the Money order was not returned to him on 13.9.1987. But the plaintiff did not produce any evidence to show that the Money Order returned to the defendant before 13.9.1987. Thus the SCC Judge held that it can be presumed that the Money Order was returned on 13.9.1987 and as such the findings of the learned Judge in Rent Control Case No. 68 of 1987 filed on 27.9.1987 can be accepted as being filed within time. 

 19. Such approach of the trial Court cannot be accepted because of the fact that in exhibit "Kha" there being no date as to when the Money Order was returned to the defendant-tenant nor there being any assertion in the defendant's written statement as to when the Money order was returned as such the presumption of return of the Money Order on 13.9.1987 is not sustainable under the law. The defendant having not stated in the written statement about the date of receipt of refused money order and no specific evidence having been adduced to that extent presumption cannot be made on the data of receipt of refused Money Order. The date which has been mentioned in the Money Order Coupon, exhibit "Kha" being the date of refusal on 9.9.1987, it cannot be said that the House Rent Control Case No. 68of 1987 which was filed on 27.9.1987 as filed within fortnight as contemplated in .section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance I986,. which was the prevailing law at the relevant period. 

 20. The other finding on the question of default as arrived at by the court below is that the Exhibit No. 8 filed by the plaintiff, which is the information slip obtained on 27.6.2000 of the Rent Control Case No. 68 of 1987 showing that the defendant defaulted in depositing the rent with the Rent Controller subsequent to filing of the House Rent Control Case, which led the Trial Court to hold that the defendant did not deposit rent in time since Exhibit 8 shows that the defendant tenant paid the rent for the month of October 1990 on the 19th day of next month. Similarly the rent for the month of November 1998 and December 1998 were deposited together on the 12th day of the next month i.e. January 1999. Again rent for the month of November and December 1997 were deposited together on the 13th day of next month i.e. January 1998. The rent for the month of November 1999 has been deposited on the 13th day of next month and the rent for the month of September 1995 has been deposited on the 5th day of next month whereas the "Bharanama" agreement dated 3.10.1979 shows that the rent is to be paid on the 5th day of next month. Thus the Trial Court held that the defendant defaulted in depositing the rent with House Rent Controller and as such he is a defaulter. 

 21. In this respect section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1986 is to be looked into. Section 19(1) and (2) of the said Ordinance are the relevant sections which attracts the present case. On perusal of the aforesaid provision of law it is clear that `when the land lord refused to accept any rent remitted by postal Money Order by a tenant of any premises, the tenant may deposit such rent within fortnight from the date on which the rent, so remitted, is retuned to the tenant by the postal authorities as undelivered and unless the landlord signifies by notice in writing to the tenant his willingness to accept any subsequent rent which becomes due in respect of such premises it may also deposit such subsequent rent within a fortnight of the date on which such rent becomes due, from the expiry of the time within which such rent is required to be paid under section 18(5) of the ordinance together with the cost of transmission by postal money order of the money deposited, to the landlord' .Similarly sub section 2 of section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1986 says 'wherein any bonafide doubt or dispute has arisen as to the person who is entitled to receive any rent referred to in section 18 in respect of any premises the tenant may deposit such rent and may continue to deposit every subsequent amount of rent which becomes due in respect of such premises until such doubt has been removed or such dispute has been settled by the decision of any competent court or by the settlement between the parties, within a fortnight of the date on which such rent becomes due or from the expiry of the time within which such rent is required to be paid under section 18,(5) of the Ordinance'. In this connection section 18 of the Ordinance is also to be looked into. Section 18says that 'no order shall be made for eviction so long the tenant pays the rent in full extent and fulfills the condition of the tenancy', Section I8(5)says that 'no tenant shall be entitled to the benefit of the section in respect of any premises unless he pays the full rent due to him in respect of such premises within stipulated date and time fixed in the contract with his land lord or in the absence of such contract by the fifteenth day of the month next following that for which the rent is payable or unless the tenant has deposited such rent or any subsequent rent in respect of the premises as provided in that section together with the cost of transmission referred to in that sub section within the time specified in sub section 1B of the said section'. So it appears that if it is taken that the agreement subsisted then the tenant is supposed t. deposit the rent within fifth day of the next following month as per the agreement date. 3.10.1979 and in case if it is taken that there is no agreement existing then the tenant is liable  to pay the rent on the 15th day of the next following month. 

 22. In the present case it appears that the tenant deposited rent for the month of October 1990 on the 19th day of November 1990; the rent of November and December 1998 were deposited together in the month of January 12th , 1999. Similarly, the rent for the month of November and December 1999 were deposited together on the 12th day of the next month i.e. January 2000. Although due to year end vacation of the Civil Court the defendant was bound to deposit the rent on the opening day of the Courts in January. So it appears that the rent for these months were not deposited with the House Rent Controller within the 15th day of the following month. So construing section 19 (I) and (2) of the ordinance along with deposit of rent for these months it appears that the defendant tenant have failed to comply with the provision of law in depositing rent within the fortnight of next following month. In this respect Mr. Deb contended that default in making deposit with the Rent Controller cannot be the criteria to determine the tenant as defaulter because of the fact that the default in depositing rent subsequent to the cause of action for the filing of the suit has no implication on the cause of action of the suit. In this respect he referred the case of M/S. Binning & Co (Bangladesh) Ltd. Vs. M/S Nasirabad Properties Ltd. reported in 40 DLR (AD)89. On the contrary Mr. Jaigirdar relying on the decision of Ramjan Ali Mistry vs. Md. Hedayetullah reported in 31 DLR (AD) 183 submits that the expression as long as tenant pays rent indicates that the point of default on the part of the tenant will be not only the date of filing of the suit but will continue till decree is passed. It does not, however, mean that if the tenant subsequent to the filing of the suit has deposited the rent with the Rent Controller the default incurred earlier is cured. On the contrary the tenant's liability for default even after the filing of the suit continues till passing of the decree, In the said decision it has been said that 'protection of the tenant against ejectment is on the fulfillment of certain conditions. He should pay rent to the full extent allowable by the Ordinance and if he does so he is protected from ejectment on the ground of default in the payment of rent.' It has further set out the terms of payment of rent that it is to paid within the time fixed by the contract and in the absence of any such contract within the fifteenth day of the month next following for which the rent is payable or he can deposit the rent with the rent controller in terms of section 19 of the Ordinance. The provision for depositing rent is in section 19 of the Ordinance wherein the provision has been made for deposit of rent to meet diverse contingencies. This provision is contained in section 19(1) of the Ordinance. It clarifies the earlier provision regarding the tender of rent by the tenant. The section says that when, the landlord has refused to accept rent in terms of section 18 of the Ordinance he is to remit it through postal money order and the tenant may deposit the rent with the Rent Controller within the fortnight of the receipt of the undelivered rent. sent through the postal authorities. Section 19(1) (la) of the Ordinance categorically says about the deposit of subsequent rent within a fortnight and section 19(2) (b) of the Ordinance says that he may continue the deposit of every subsequent amount of rent, which becomes due in respect of such premises, within a fortnight of the date in which such rent becomes due until such doubt has been removed or such dispute has been settled by the decision of any competent court or by settlement between the parties. 

 23. On perusal of the decision as referred to by Mr. Deb reported in 40 DLR (AD) 89 it appears that the same is not applicable in this particular case. Therein the Appellate. Division held that the statutory restriction relating to payment of monthly rent within 15th  day of the next month, if disregarded by the tenant that will disentitle him to the protection against eviction for default in payment of rent. Mere acceptance of rent by the landlord without objection or protest is not sufficient to constitute waiver. Mr. Deb relied on paragraph No.7 of the said decision and on perusal of the some it appears that that it was not the decision of the honorable court rather the same is the submission made by the learned Advocate of the respondents. Rather in paragraph No. 8 of the said decision it has been held by the Appellate Division "  We are unable to accept the contention that the defendant petitioner is not a defaulter." In the said decision, it has been held that payment of rent in lump for two/three months together does not save a tenant from the mischief of default. 

 Thus, by cross referring these two decisions reported in 40DLR (AD) 89 and 31 DLR (AD) 183 and on referring through the sections 19(1) and (2) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1986 I am of the view that the defendant tenant having not deposited the rent subsequent to filing of the House Rent Control Case No. 68 of 1987 in accordance with law i.e. within the fortnight of the next following month the tenant became a defaulter. Moreover, law provides that the defendant is to pay rent to the landlord or deposit the same with the House Rent Controller wither the period as stipulated in the contract and in the absence of any contract within fortnight of the next following month. Thus the submissions of Mr. Dev, the learned Advocate for the defendant/petitioners that the default in depositing rent subsequent to filing of the suit does not entitle the landlord to a decree for eviction is of no substance, meaning that to get the protection of law the tenant is to pay or deposit the rent in accordance with law till the disposal of the eviction suit either to the landlord or to the House Rent. Controller within the stipulated period of time in the contract or in the absence of contract within fortnight of the next following month, as contemplated in section 18(5) and 19(1) and (2) of the Ordinance failing which the tenant cannot avoid his liability of being a defaulter and as such liable to be evicted. Thus in the present case the tenant having failed to deposit the rent with the House Rent Controller for the month as mentioned above within fortnight of the following month, he is a defaulter in the eye of law and once a defaulter is always a defaulter. Hence he cannot avoid the liability of being evicted.
